keyVerseText: And he said, Go into the city to such a man, and say unto him, The Master saith, My time is at hand; I will keep the passover at thy house with my disciples.
rootMeaning: The Greek noun δεῖνα (deîna) likely derives from the same root as δεινῶς (deinōs), which means 'grievously' or 'terribly.' This etymological connection suggests a nuance of something striking or fearfully strange, possibly reflecting the idea of forgetting or withholding a name out of reverence or caution. Thus, beyond its common English gloss as 'such a man,' δεῖνα carries an undertone of an unspecified or notable person whose identity is either unknown or intentionally left vague.
usageInScripture: The word δεῖνα occurs only once in the New Testament, specifically in Matthew 26:18, where it is translated as 'such a man.' This consistent translation highlights its use as a euphemism or placeholder for an individual whose name is either not known or not disclosed. The singular occurrence and the lexical note that it is used 'when the person is not specified' reveal that δεῖνα functions primarily as a discreet or indirect reference to a particular person in narrative contexts.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding δεῖνα as a term that refers to an unnamed or unspecified person invites reflection on the humility and discretion often present in biblical narratives. The choice to use such a term rather than a name underscores the mystery and sovereignty of God’s plan, where not all details are revealed to us. It also reminds believers that God’s work involves ordinary, sometimes hidden individuals who play crucial roles in His redemptive story. This aligns with the biblical theme that God often works through the seemingly insignificant or unknown to accomplish His purposes, pointing ultimately to Christ as the central figure of revelation.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 26:18, Jesus instructs His disciples to go to 'such a man' to prepare the Passover. The use of δεῖνα here emphasizes the discreet and confidential nature of the arrangement, underscoring the seriousness and urgency of the moment. By referring to the host anonymously, the text invites readers to focus on the significance of the event—the institution of the Lord’s Supper—rather than on the identity of the individual. This highlights the divine orchestration behind the scenes, where God’s plan unfolds through ordinary people in ways that invite faith and trust.
